lesson.title: Reading for synonyms and sentence endings

learning_objectives.en: Match the logic and grammar of two clause halves and recognise paraphrases.
learning_objectives.vi: Ghép hai nửa câu theo ngữ nghĩa và ngữ pháp, nhận biết diễn đạt lại.

content.en: Identify the meaning and grammatical structure of the first half before reading endings. The ending must fit the whole sentence, and one text may express the same idea using different vocabulary.
content.vi: Xác định ý và cấu trúc của nửa đầu trước khi xem nửa sau. Nửa sau phải khớp toàn câu; văn bản có thể dùng từ đồng nghĩa khác.

strategies.en: Predict whether the gap needs a person, action or result, then scan for the matching idea. Extra endings are distractors.
strategies.vi: Dự đoán thiếu người, hành động hay kết quả rồi mới quét ý tương ứng. Phương án thừa là distractor.

common_mistakes.wrong: Any ending with similar vocabulary is correct
common_mistakes.correct: Check meaning, grammar and source evidence

reason.en: Distractors can share vocabulary but contradict cause and effect.
reason.vi: Phương án nhiễu có từ tương tự nhưng sai quan hệ nguyên nhân–kết quả.

passages.title: Why small cafés close – and why some survive
passages.text:
[A] Opening a café is one of the most popular choices for first-time business owners, and also one of the riskiest. In the fictional city of Larkford, records show that nearly half of new cafés close within three years. Researchers at the local business school interviewed the owners of forty cafés – some that had failed and some that were still trading – to understand what made the difference.

[B] Rent was the most frequently mentioned problem. Owners who chose busy shopping streets often paid three or four times more than those in quieter residential areas, and many underestimated how many cups of coffee they would need to sell each day simply to cover their costs. Several successful owners said they had deliberately chosen cheaper locations near offices or schools, where they could build a regular group of customers.

[C] Market research also mattered. Owners who failed were more likely to have opened the kind of café they personally liked, without checking whether local people wanted it. One owner opened an expensive specialist coffee shop in an area where most residents were retired and preferred tea and cake at lower prices. By contrast, survivors had usually spent weeks observing the area, counting passers-by and talking to potential customers before signing a lease.

[D] Staff turnover was a hidden cost. Cafés that paid only the minimum wage and offered no training found that employees left within a few months, which meant constant recruitment and inconsistent service. Owners of long-lasting cafés often described their staff as the main reason customers returned, and several paid above the minimum wage despite their small profit margins.

[E] Finally, the survivors were more willing to change. Many had added services after opening – breakfast menus for office workers, evening events, delivery or space for small meetings – once they had learned what their customers needed. The researchers concluded that a café’s success depends less on its first idea than on how quickly the owner can learn and adapt. As one long-standing owner put it, the menu on the wall today looks almost nothing like the one she started with.

passages.title: Learning on the job: apprenticeships return
passages.text:
[A] For many years, young people in the fictional country of Carvia were told that a university degree was the safest route to a good career. Apprenticeships – in which trainees work for an employer while studying part-time – were often seen as a second choice for those who did not do well at school. That view is now changing. Over the past five years, the number of apprenticeships in Carvia has risen by forty per cent, and they now cover areas such as software engineering, accounting and healthcare as well as traditional trades.

[B] One obvious attraction is cost. Apprentices are paid a salary from the first day, and their training fees are covered by the employer and the government, so most finish without any debt. University graduates in Carvia, by contrast, leave with an average debt equal to about two years’ starting salary.

[C] Employers also report benefits. A survey of three hundred companies found that apprentices were more likely than graduate recruits to stay with the company for at least five years. Some managers believe this is because apprentices feel loyal to an employer that invested in them; others suggest that they simply have a clearer idea of the job before they commit to it.

[D] Not everyone is convinced. Some teachers argue that apprenticeships force young people to choose a career too early, at sixteen or eighteen, when many do not yet know what they want to do. A degree, they say, keeps more options open. In the view of the national students’ association, the best system would make it easier to move between the two routes, so that an apprentice could later go to university and a graduate could retrain through an apprenticeship.

[E] Whatever the debate, demand is rising. In the most popular programmes, there are now more than ten applicants for every place, which suggests that apprenticeships are no longer seen as an easy option. Several employers have started visiting secondary schools to explain what apprentices actually do, hoping to reach students before they make their final choice about university.
